title: Are you the Coming One?
sum: The mission speech is over, and a new section begins: how will people respond to Jesus? First comes a question from prison. John the Baptist, who had announced a fiery judge, hears of a Messiah who heals and eats with sinners, and asks whether Jesus is really the one. Jesus answers with Isaiah's signs of God's coming rescue and then praises John: he is more than a prophet, the Elijah Malachi promised, and yet the smallest in the kingdom is greater.

The mood darkens. "This generation" will dance to no tune: it called John possessed and Jesus a glutton. Jesus pronounces woes on the lake towns that saw most of his works and did not repent. Then the tone turns again, to thanks: the Father has shown these things to little children. The chapter ends with one of the best-loved sayings in the Gospels, Wisdom's invitation in Jesus' mouth: "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down."
readings: John's question rings true: a prisoner who expected judgment wonders about a Messiah of mercy. The insults ("glutton," "drunkard," "friend of sinners") are the kind of thing the church would not invent, so most historians count them as memories of how people saw Jesus. The towns named are real places within a few miles of each other on the north shore of the lake.

Chapter 11 opens a long section (11–12) on rejection. Matthew frames it with "works": "the Messiah's works" (11:2) and wisdom proved right "by the things she does" (11:19). John, "this generation," the towns, the wise and the little children each respond differently. The section moves from question to rejection to invitation, and the invitation leads straight into two Sabbath stories.

Many scholars see Matthew presenting Jesus as God's Wisdom in person. Wisdom is rejected (11:19), hides and reveals (11:25–27), and calls the weary to her yoke (11:28–30), as in Proverbs 1, 8 and 9 and in Sirach 51. Jesus is not only Wisdom's prophet; he speaks as Wisdom herself.

views.H: John's arrest by Herod Antipas is confirmed by Josephus, who places it at Machaerus. John's question and Jesus' answer fit the hopes of the time: a Dead Sea Scroll (4Q521) links healing, raising the dead and good news for the poor with God's anointed. Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are excavated sites a few miles apart.
views.C: Matthew joins Mark's outline with sayings he shares with Luke (often called Q): John's question and Jesus' praise (Luke 7:18–35), the woes (Luke 10:13–15), the thanksgiving (Luke 10:21–22). Only Matthew has 11:28–30, which many think he drew from his own tradition or composed from Wisdom texts like Sirach 51. Matthew's changes include "works" in 11:19 for Luke's "children."
views.L: The second discourse ends with the formula of 11:1, and the narrative turns to Israel's response. Key words tie the chapter together: works, coming, rest. The "rest" of 11:28–29 leads into the Sabbath, the day of rest, in chapter 12.
views.J: Every part of this chapter belongs to Jewish debate: Elijah's return (Malachi 4:5–6; Sirach 48:10), Wisdom's invitation (Sirach 51), the "yoke of the kingdom of heaven" taken on in the Shema (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). Jewish scholars note that Jesus speaks as a Jewish teacher offering his own interpretation of Torah as a yoke. The woes on Galilean towns are prophetic warnings to Jesus' own people, in the style of Amos and Jeremiah.
views.T: The fathers read John's question as asked for his disciples' sake. 11:27 was central in the debates over the Trinity in the 300s. 11:28–30 has been read in the liturgy and prayer for centuries; the Anglican Book of Common Prayer places it among the "comfortable words" spoken before Communion.

deep.h: John and Jesus: two ministries, one rejection
deep.b:
Matthew sets John and Jesus side by side throughout. Both preach "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near" (3:2; 4:17). Both are opposed by Pharisees (3:7; 12:14). Both will be handed over and killed (14:10; 27:26). Chapter 11 states the parallel in a parable: John came fasting, Jesus came feasting, and "this generation" rejected both (11:16–19).

Yet they are not equal. John is the greatest of those born of women, but he stands at the threshold. He prepares the way; Jesus is the way's goal. John asks; Jesus answers. John is Elijah; Jesus is the one Elijah announces. Matthew's first readers, some of whom may have known followers of John (Acts 19:1–7), would hear both honor for John and a clear statement of his place.

Most of this chapter has a parallel in Luke, but in a different order: John's question and Jesus' praise of John come in Luke 7:18–35; the saying about the violent in Luke 16:16; the woes on the towns in Luke 10:13–15, during the mission of the seventy-two; and the thanksgiving in Luke 10:21–22. Matthew gathers them into one chapter on response and rejection. Differences include Matthew's "works" for Luke's "children" (11:19), Matthew's Elijah saying (11:14, only in Matthew), and the invitation of 11:28–30, which Luke does not have.

echoes: Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5–6; Exodus 23:20; Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 61:1; Isaiah 14:13–15; Genesis 19:24–28; Deuteronomy 21:20; Proverbs 9:1–6; Jeremiah 6:16; Sirach 51:23–27; Psalm 118:26; Luke 7:18–35; Luke 10:13–15; Luke 10:21–22; Luke 16:16; Mark 1:2; John 1:21; 17:10–13

settings.to: John's disciples, sent from prison, and through them John himself
settings.when: while John was held by Herod Antipas, after news of Jesus' healings
settings.why: Jesus does not say "yes" outright. He points John to what is happening and lets Isaiah's promises speak. For John, who had expected the axe and the fire (3:10–12), the answer explains that God's rescue comes first as healing and good news, and it gently warns him not to stumble. Knowing that the hearers are John's own disciples, who might follow Jesus or not, sharpens the blessing in 11:6.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, some of whom may have known followers of John (Acts 19:1–7), the scene settled John's place: he pointed to Jesus.

settings.to: the crowds in Galilee who had gone out to hear John
settings.when: just after John's messengers left
settings.why: Jesus defends John before people who may have thought less of him because of his question. He reminds them why they went into the wilderness and tells them who John really was: more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1, and Elijah for those ready to receive it.
settings.readers: For Matthew's community, some of whom may have known followers of John, the passage honored John while setting him below the smallest in the kingdom.
views: Most commentators read 11:12 as a word about opposition: the kingdom suffers violence, as John's imprisonment shows.
Others, with many fathers and Luke 16:16, read it of people pressing eagerly into the kingdom.

settings.what: The parable of the children in the marketplace
settings.to: the same crowds, continuing his words about John
settings.when: just after he spoke about John
settings.why: Jesus compares "this generation" to children in a town square who will join neither a wedding game nor a funeral game. John came fasting and was called possessed; Jesus came eating and drinking and was called a glutton. The hearers would recognize the street game and then see themselves in the sulking children.
settings.readers: For Matthew's community, in conflict with the synagogue, the parable explained why many in Israel had accepted neither John nor Jesus.
views: Luke has the same parable in the same setting, after John's question (Luke 7:31–35), but ends with wisdom's "children" rather than her works.

settings.what: The woes on the lake towns
settings.to: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, addressed as if present, in the hearing of the crowds
settings.when: after most of his acts of power had been done there, and they had not repented
settings.why: These are prophetic laments and warnings, in the style of the prophets' oracles against cities. They were meant to shock the towns that had seen the most into turning: if pagan Tyre, Sidon and even Sodom would have repented, how much more should they. Knowing that Capernaum was Jesus' own base makes the words sharper: privilege brings responsibility.
views: Luke places these woes in a different setting, in Jesus' charge to the seventy-two before he sends them out (Luke 10:13–15).
settings.readers: For Matthew's first readers after AD 70, the towns' indifference was part of the larger story of Israel's mixed response, and a warning to the church not to take its own privileges for granted.

settings.to: God the Father, spoken aloud in the hearing of the disciples and the crowd
settings.when: "at that time," right after the woes
settings.why: Jesus thanks the Father that the truth has gone to the "little children" rather than to the "wise." Spoken in the hearing of his followers, mostly ordinary people from Galilee, it tells them that God's choice of them is not a mistake. It then claims a unique relation between Father and Son: what the disciples know of God they know through Jesus.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, a minority looked down on by learned opponents, heard that their simplicity was God's choice, not their disgrace.
views: Luke sets this prayer when the seventy-two return rejoicing from their mission, and Jesus speaks the next words privately to the disciples (Luke 10:17–24).

settings.to: "all of you who are worn out and loaded down": the crowds, especially ordinary people burdened by daily toil and by demanding religious teaching
settings.when: at the end of the chapter, after the thanksgiving
settings.why: Jesus offers himself as the teacher whose yoke is kind. His hearers knew the language of taking on a teacher's or the Torah's yoke. The invitation does not cancel the law (5:17–20) but offers it through a gentle teacher, in contrast to teachers who load others and lift no finger (23:4). Knowing the hearers were peasants and laborers gives "worn out" its literal force too.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, between the synagogue's yoke of Torah and the yoke of Christ, heard that following Jesus is the true way of keeping God's will, and that it gives rest.
views: Many read the burdens as strict religious rules laid on people (23:4).
Others read them more widely, as the toil, sin and suffering of life, and Jesus' rest as rest with God.

traditions.q: Does Matthew 11:25–27 mean that God chooses who will come to know him?
views: Yes. Calvin read 11:25–27 as showing that faith comes from God's free choice, not from human wisdom; the Westminster Confession and the Canons of Dort teach that God elects some to life by grace alone, and the Son reveals the Father to those the Father has given him.

God hides the truth from those who are "wise" in their own eyes and reveals it to the humble. Wesley read the passage as God's response to pride, not an eternal decree that passes some people by; grace is offered to all, and people can refuse it.

God reveals himself freely to the humble, and no one can know the Father apart from the Son. Catholic theologians differ on how grace and freedom fit together (Thomists following Aquinas, Molinists following Molina), but agree that God wills all to be saved and predestines no one to hell (Catechism 1037).

Knowledge of God is a gift given to the humble and pure in heart. Salvation is a cooperation (synergy) of God's grace and human freedom; Orthodox teachers reject any idea of God choosing some for damnation.

God's election is a comfort to believers, and faith is wholly God's gift through the word; but Lutherans do not teach that God chooses anyone for damnation. Those who are lost reject the grace offered to them, as the Formula of Concord teaches.

title: Lord of the Sabbath
sum: Right after offering rest, Jesus clashes with Pharisees over the day of rest. His hungry disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, and he defends them with David, the temple and Hosea: "Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice" (12:7). He heals a man with a withered hand in a synagogue, and the Pharisees begin to plan his death. Jesus withdraws, and Matthew quotes Isaiah's servant who will not quarrel or shout, who will not break a crushed reed.

When Jesus frees a blind and mute man from a demon, the crowds wonder whether he is the Son of David, but the Pharisees say he drives out demons by Beelzebul. Jesus answers that a kingdom divided cannot stand, that he is tying up the strong man, and that speaking against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. Asked for a sign, he offers only the sign of Jonah. The chapter ends with his family standing outside, and Jesus pointing to his disciples: "Look! My mother and my brothers!" (12:49)
readings: Sabbath debates were real in Jesus' time, and Jewish groups disagreed about what counted as work. The charge that Jesus used demonic power is very likely historical: no one would invent an accusation like that against their master, and it shows that even opponents agreed he did exorcisms.

Chapter 12 turns rejection into open hostility. The Pharisees go from objecting (12:2) to plotting (12:14) to calling Jesus demonic (12:24). Matthew answers with Isaiah's gentle servant (12:18–21) and with Jesus' claims: something greater than the temple, than Jonah, than Solomon. The chapter ends by naming Jesus' true family: those who do the Father's will.

The Beelzebul debate shows the kingdom as a war with Satan. Jesus binds the strong man and plunders his house. There is no neutral ground: "Whoever is not with me is against me." The returning spirits warn that an empty, cleaned house is not enough.

views.H: Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law, including Sabbath rules. Later rabbinic texts list 39 kinds of forbidden work and allow saving a life on the Sabbath, but they record debates about animals and lesser help, and the Dead Sea community was stricter than the Pharisees (Damascus Document 11). Exorcism was widely practiced by Jews in the first century, as Josephus reports.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 2:23–3:35 with changes. He adds the temple argument and Hosea 6:6 (12:5–7), the sheep in a pit (12:11–12, compare Luke 14:5), the long Isaiah quotation (12:18–21), and sayings shared with Luke on the strong man, the sign of Jonah and the returning spirit (Luke 11:14–32). Matthew leaves out Mark's note that Jesus' family thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21).
views.L: Matthew's longest Old Testament quotation stands at the center of the chapter (12:18–21), framing the conflict: Jesus is God's chosen servant on whom the Spirit rests, so to call his work Satan's is to speak against the Spirit. The theme of "greater" runs through the chapter: greater than the temple (12:6), Jonah (12:41) and Solomon (12:42).
views.J: Jewish readers note that Jesus argues in rabbinic style: from Scripture (David, the priests), from a lesser case to a greater one (the sheep), and with the principle of mercy. Many scholars, Jewish and Christian, think Jesus' Sabbath practice stayed within the range of Jewish debate; the plot to kill him over it reflects the bitter conflicts of Matthew's own day. The saying about the Spirit has a parallel in Jewish teaching that some sins are not atoned for (Mishnah Yoma 8:8–9).
views.T: Churches have read 12:1–8 in debates about Sunday and the Sabbath, 12:31–32 in teaching about the unforgivable sin, 12:32 ("the age to come") in debates about purgatory, and 12:46–50 in debates about Mary and Jesus' brothers. See the cards below.

deep.b:
Keeping the Sabbath was a mark of Jewish identity, honored even by Jews far from the land. The Torah forbade work but did not define it in detail. Later the Mishnah listed 39 main kinds of work, including reaping and threshing (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). Rubbing grain in the hand could count as both. Groups differed: the Damascus Document forbids helping an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath, while later rabbis allowed some help. All agreed that danger to human life sets aside the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6).

Jesus does not say the Sabbath is abolished. He argues about what it is for: doing good and showing mercy. Matthew's version, more than Mark's, shows Jesus giving reasons from Scripture, as a teacher in a Jewish debate would.

The name appears in the New Testament only in the Gospels. It probably goes back to Baal-zebub, "lord of flies," the god of Ekron in 2 Kings 1:2, itself perhaps a mocking change of Baal-zebul, "Baal the prince." By Jesus' time it was a name for the ruler of the demons, whom Jesus identifies with Satan (12:26). The charge that Jesus worked by evil power appears again in later Jewish and pagan polemic: the Babylonian Talmud says Jesus "practiced sorcery" (Sanhedrin 43a), and the pagan critic Celsus claimed he had learned magic in Egypt (Origen, Against Celsus 1.28). This shows how widely his exorcisms were known.

echoes: 1 Samuel 21:1–6; Leviticus 24:5–9; Numbers 28:9–10; Hosea 6:6; Deuteronomy 23:25; Isaiah 42:1–4; Isaiah 49:3; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 53:9; 2 Kings 1:2; Isaiah 49:24–25; Exodus 8:19; Jonah 1:17; Jonah 3:5; 1 Kings 10:1–10; Mark 2:23–3:35; Luke 6:1–11; Luke 11:14–32; Luke 6:43–45; Luke 8:19–21; 3:17; 9:13; 16:4; 17:5

settings.to: Pharisees who saw his disciples picking and eating grain
settings.when: on a Sabbath, walking through grainfields in Galilee
settings.why: The Pharisees raise a real legal question, and Jesus answers in kind, with Scripture: David's hungry men, the priests who work in the temple on the Sabbath, and Hosea 6:6. To hearers who knew the law, he argues that need and mercy shape how the Sabbath is kept, and he ends with a claim about himself: the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
settings.readers: Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers, who still kept the Sabbath, learned from this how to keep it: with mercy, not as a contest of strictness.

settings.what: The saying about the sheep in a pit
settings.to: Pharisees in the synagogue who asked whether healing on the Sabbath is allowed, "so that they could accuse him"
settings.when: the same Sabbath, in their synagogue, with the man with the withered hand present
settings.why: Jesus argues from a lesser case to a greater one: if you would lift a sheep out of a pit, how much more should you help a person. Many hearers did rescue animals on the Sabbath, though stricter groups did not (Damascus Document 11). The point lands before a crowd watching to see what he will do.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, the rule "doing good on the Sabbath is allowed" (12:12) summed up how the Sabbath should be kept.

settings.by: Matthew, quoting Isaiah 42:1–4 in a form close to the Hebrew but not exactly any known text
settings.to: Matthew's readers
settings.when: inserted after Jesus withdraws and orders people not to make him known
settings.why: Isaiah's words were first addressed to Israel facing or in exile (most scholars date Isaiah 40–55 to the exile; traditional readers to Isaiah of Jerusalem), about the servant whom God would use to bring justice to the nations. Matthew applies them to Jesus' quiet way: he withdraws instead of fighting, and he heals the weak. The quotation also answers the next scene: the Spirit is on Jesus, so the charge of Beelzebul is a charge against God's Spirit.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, many of whom were reaching out to the nations, heard that this mission was already in Isaiah.
views: In Isaiah, the servant in 42:1 is often understood as Israel (compare Isaiah 41:8), or Israel's faithful remnant.
Many Christian readers, and some Jewish interpreters (the Targum applies 42:1 to the Messiah), read it of one coming figure.

settings.what: Jesus' answer to the Beelzebul charge
settings.to: the Pharisees who said he drove out demons by Beelzebul, with the amazed crowds listening
settings.when: just after he healed a blind and mute man
settings.why: The crowds were asking whether Jesus is the Son of David; the Pharisees answered by calling his power demonic. Jesus replies with logic (a divided kingdom falls), with a challenge ("your sons" also drive out demons), and with a picture (the strong man tied up). He then warns them that their words reveal what is in their hearts, and that they will answer for them on judgment day.
settings.readers: Matthew's community, whose own healers may have faced similar charges (10:25), heard that rejecting the Spirit's work is a grave thing.

settings.what: The sign of Jonah and the returning spirit
settings.to: some scribes and Pharisees who asked for a sign
settings.when: right after the Beelzebul debate
settings.why: They ask for proof after already seeing healings and exorcisms. Jesus refuses any sign except Jonah: his three days in the earth, and his call to repent. The pagan people of Nineveh and the queen of the south will judge this generation, because they responded to less. The story of the returning spirit warns that a cleaned-up life with nothing in it ends worse than it began.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers after the resurrection, the "sign of Jonah" pointed to Easter, and the judgment of "this generation" to the disaster of AD 70.

settings.what: Jesus' words about his true family
settings.to: the person who told him his mother and brothers were outside, and the crowd and disciples around him
settings.when: while he was still speaking to the crowds
settings.why: Family loyalty was a basic duty. Jesus does not reject his family, but he names a new family whose bond is doing the Father's will. Spoken in front of disciples who had left homes and families (4:22; 10:37), it promises them a family they have not lost.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, some cut off from their own families for following Jesus (10:35–36), heard that the church is their family.

traditions.q: Do Christians need to keep the seventh-day Sabbath?
views: Yes. The Sabbath is part of God's moral law from creation. Jesus kept the Sabbath and as "Lord of the Sabbath" freed it from human rules, not from God's command; Christians should rest and worship on Saturday.
Sunday, the day of the resurrection, fulfills the Sabbath for Christians. The Sabbath command is kept by worship and rest on the Lord's Day, which the church has observed from the beginning.
The fourth commandment is a moral law for all times, but since the resurrection the day has changed to the first day of the week, the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy by rest and worship.
The Sabbath laws of Moses do not bind Christians. The church sets Sunday for public worship as a matter of good order, and the point of the commandment is to hear God's word.
Many Baptists keep Sunday as the Lord's Day for worship and rest. Confessions differ on how strictly it is a Sabbath: the 1689 Confession calls it the Christian Sabbath.

traditions.q: What is the sin against the Holy Spirit that will not be forgiven (12:31–32)?
views: It is deliberately refusing to accept God's mercy through repentance. God's mercy has no limits, but a person who refuses it shuts himself off from forgiveness.

Chrysostom explained that the Pharisees had no excuse of ignorance: they saw the Spirit's plain works and called them demonic. Orthodox teachers describe the sin as hardened resistance to known truth, which shuts out repentance; it is unforgivable because it is not repented of.
Calvin taught that it is a knowing, malicious rejection of truth by someone the Spirit has enlightened. Those who commit it never seek forgiveness.
Wesley explained it narrowly as the Pharisees' sin: saying that the works Jesus did by the Spirit of God were done by the devil.
Lutheran teachers define it as a final, malicious rejection of the gospel by someone the Spirit has convinced of its truth. Such a person does not seek forgiveness, so it is never received.

traditions.q: Does "not in the age that is coming" (12:32) mean some sins are forgiven after death?
views: Yes. Gregory the Great (Dialogues 4.39, quoted in Catechism 1031) reasoned from this verse that some sins can be forgiven in the age to come, and the church teaches a final purification, purgatory, for those who die in God's grace but are not fully purified.
The church prays for the dead, trusting that God may grant them mercy, but most Orthodox teachers do not accept the Catholic teaching on purgatory as a place of satisfying punishment.
No. The verse means only that this sin will never be forgiven. The Smalcald Articles reject purgatory as having no support in Scripture.
No. "Not in this age and not in the age that is coming" is a way of saying "never." After death, souls go at once to heaven or to hell.
The Thirty-nine Articles reject "the Romish doctrine concerning purgatory," though some Anglicans pray for the dead.

Close relatives (Catechism 500); in the Western tradition since Jerome, usually cousins. Mary remained a virgin all her life; Jerome argued that "brothers" can mean kin, as Abraham calls Lot his brother.
Sons of Joseph from an earlier marriage, so Jesus' stepbrothers. This view is found in the Protevangelium of James and defended by Epiphanius, and Mary is honored as ever-virgin.
Luther honored Mary as ever-virgin, and the Smalcald Articles call her "ever virgin"; many Lutherans today leave the question open.
Calvin did not claim that Mary had other children and warned against speculation; many Reformed and other Protestant scholars today read them as Mary and Joseph's sons.
Most Baptists read the brothers as children born to Mary and Joseph after Jesus, the plain meaning of the words. This view goes back to Tertullian and to Helvidius, whom Jerome answered.

title: Parables of the Kingdom
sum: This is the third of Jesus' five long speeches in Matthew. Sitting in a boat, Jesus teaches the crowds on the shore in parables: short stories from farming, baking, fishing and trade. A farmer sows seed on four kinds of ground. An enemy sows weeds among the wheat. A tiny mustard seed becomes a tree; a little yeast works through a huge batch of dough. Between the stories, Jesus tells his disciples why he speaks in parables, quoting Isaiah about people who look but do not see, and explains the sower and the weeds.

Then, to the disciples alone, come three more: treasure hidden in a field, a merchant who finds one priceless pearl, and a net that gathers every kind of fish. The speech ends with the disciples saying they understand, and Jesus describing a scribe trained for the kingdom, who brings out new and old treasures. Afterward, in his hometown, people are amazed but take offense: isn't this the builder's son? Jesus did not do many acts of power there because of their unbelief.
readings: Most scholars agree that parables were Jesus' most typical way of teaching, and the sower, mustard seed, yeast, treasure and pearl are widely judged to go back to him. They describe God's kingdom as small and hidden now, but sure to grow and worth everything.

Matthew builds a careful speech: four parables to the crowd, then a turn to the house and three parables to the disciples, with explanations in between. Many see paired parables (mustard seed and yeast; treasure and pearl) and two allegories explained in detail (the sower and the weeds). The speech explains why so many in chapters 11–12 rejected Jesus.
The weeds and the net speak to a mixed community where good and bad live together until the end. Matthew's readers would hear warnings against judging too soon and against assuming they are wheat.

views.H: The parables use everyday life in Galilee: sowing by broadcasting seed (perhaps before plowing, as Jeremias argued), weeds that look like wheat, fishing with dragnets on the lake, hiding treasure in the ground in times of war. The yields of thirty to a hundredfold are high but not impossible for very good land; Genesis 26:12 describes a hundredfold harvest as God's blessing.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 4:1–34 for the sower, its explanation and the mustard seed, and shares the yeast with Luke 13:20–21. The weeds, treasure, pearl, net and the trained scribe are found only in Matthew. Versions of several parables appear in the Gospel of Thomas, which some scholars use to study earlier forms. Many scholars think the detailed explanations (13:18–23, 36–43) reflect the early church's teaching, while others defend them as Jesus' own.
views.L: This is Matthew's third discourse, ending with "When Jesus finished these parables" (13:53). It falls at the center of the Gospel. The speech moves from crowd to disciples, from public to private, and from parable to explanation. The scene at Nazareth that follows shows the hardening the speech describes.
views.J: Parables (Hebrew mashal) were a common Jewish teaching form; the rabbis later told hundreds of them, many about a king. Jewish readers note that Jesus' parables share this world. The quotation from Isaiah 6 had been used before to explain Israel's unbelief, and Christians later used it to present Jews as rejected by God, a use the Catholic Church disowned when it taught that Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4).
views.T: The fathers read the parables as pictures of the church and the soul. Augustine used the weeds to argue that the church on earth is a mixed body, an idea that shaped centuries of debate about church discipline and religious freedom (see the card below). Mystics and preachers have loved the treasure and the pearl as pictures of giving everything for God.

deep.b:
Matthew 13:10–17 raises a hard question: do parables reveal or hide? Mark says Jesus spoke in parables "so that" outsiders would not understand (Mark 4:12). Matthew writes "because" (13:13): people already do not see, so Jesus speaks in a way that invites those who want to understand and leaves others where they are. Then Matthew quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 in full as being fulfilled.

The answer seems to be both. Parables are open stories that draw listeners in, but they need the key of discipleship. "Let anyone who has ears listen" (13:9) is an invitation, not a lock. The disciples are blessed not because they are clever but because they stay and ask.

For centuries, Christian readers explained every detail of a parable as a symbol. Around 1900 Adolf Jülicher argued that Jesus' parables each make only one main point, and that allegory came later. Joachim Jeremias built on this, trying to recover the original settings. More recent scholars, including Klyne Snodgrass and Jewish scholars of rabbinic parables, point out that Jewish parables often mix story and allegory, so allegory in Jesus' parables need not be late. Matthew himself explains two parables in detail.

The chapter ends with Jesus rejected at home. Matthew follows Mark 6:1–6 but makes two changes: Jesus is "the builder's son," not "the builder" (Mark 6:3), and Matthew says he "did not do many" acts of power there rather than that he "could not." Luke tells a fuller version at the start of Jesus' ministry (Luke 4:16–30). A tektōn worked with wood or stone; nearby Sepphoris was being rebuilt in Jesus' youth.

echoes: Isaiah 6:9–10; Psalm 78:2; Genesis 26:12; Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12; Ezekiel 31:6; Genesis 18:6; Daniel 12:3; Zephaniah 1:3; Proverbs 2:4; Mark 4:1–34; Luke 8:4–18; Luke 13:18–21; Mark 6:1–6; Luke 4:16–30; John 4:44; 3:12; 8:12; 10:24–25; 12:46–50; 24:31; 25:32

settings.to: the large crowds standing on the shore, with Jesus sitting in a boat
settings.when: the same day, by the lake
settings.why: Many in the crowd were farmers who knew that much seed is lost to paths, rocks and thorns. The story ends surprisingly: the good soil yields thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. Told to a crowd after the rejections of chapters 11–12, it says that despite failure, God's word will bear a great harvest. It ends with a call to listen.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, small and opposed, heard reassurance that the word they preached would still bear fruit.

settings.to: his disciples, privately, after they came and asked him
settings.when: the same day, after the sower
settings.why: Jesus tells those who have stayed with him that they have been given to know the secrets of the kingdom. The Isaiah quotation explains why many others have not understood. For disciples who had seen opposition grow, it says that this was foreseen, and calls them blessed for seeing what prophets longed to see.
settings.readers: Matthew's community, explaining why most of their people did not believe, found the answer in Isaiah.

settings.to: his disciples, privately
settings.when: the same day, after the sower
settings.why: Jesus explains the four soils as four ways of hearing: the word snatched away, received with joy but dropped under pressure, choked by worries and wealth, and heard, understood and fruitful. The point for the disciples is to be the good soil.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, facing persecution ("hardship or persecution," 13:21) and the pull of wealth, the explanation was a check-up on their own hearts.
views: Some scholars defend the explanation as Jesus' own, noting that Jewish parables were often explained.
Others, following Jeremias, think it reflects the early church's preaching, since its words are typical of later Christian vocabulary.

settings.to: the large crowds standing on the shore, with Jesus sitting in a boat
settings.when: the same day, by the lake
settings.why: Farmers knew darnel, a weed that looks like wheat until it heads out. Sowing it in someone's field was a known act of revenge; Roman law later dealt with it. To hearers who expected the Messiah to clear out the wicked at once, the parable says: not yet. Good and bad grow together until the harvest.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, in a mixed world and a mixed church, heard a warning against pulling up others too soon.

settings.what: The parable of the mustard seed
settings.to: the large crowds standing on the shore, with Jesus sitting in a boat
settings.when: the same day, by the lake
settings.why: The mustard seed was proverbially tiny. Jesus says the kingdom starts that small but becomes a tree where birds nest, words that echo Daniel and Ezekiel's picture of a great kingdom sheltering the nations. To a crowd watching a small band around a Galilean teacher, it promised a great result.
settings.readers: Luke puts this parable later, in a synagogue (Luke 13:18–19). Matthew's readers, a small movement, heard that their beginnings did not show their end.

settings.to: the large crowds standing on the shore, with Jesus sitting in a boat
settings.when: the same day, by the lake
settings.why: A woman hides a little yeast in three measures of flour, enough to feed perhaps a hundred people, as when Sarah baked for Abraham's guests (Genesis 18:6). The hidden yeast works through it all. To the crowd, it pictured the kingdom's quiet, unstoppable power.
settings.readers: In Luke the yeast parable follows the mustard seed in the same place (Luke 13:20–21). Matthew's readers heard that the kingdom works from within.
views: Most readers see the yeast as a positive picture of the kingdom spreading.
Some, noting that yeast usually stands for corruption (16:6; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8), argue the parable is meant to shock, or describes evil spreading in the church; Scofield took this view.

settings.what: Matthew's comment and quotation of Psalm 78
settings.to: Matthew's readers
settings.when: after the crowd parables
settings.why: Psalm 78 was spoken by Asaph to retell Israel's history as a lesson. Matthew calls Asaph "the prophet" (2 Chronicles 29:30 calls him a visionary) and reads his words as fulfilled in Jesus, who reveals "things hidden since the beginning."
settings.readers: Matthew's readers learned that Jesus' parables were part of God's plan announced in Scripture.

settings.to: his disciples, privately, in the house, after they asked
settings.when: the same day, after the crowds were sent away
settings.why: Jesus explains the weeds as an allegory of the end: the Son of Man sows, the field is the world, the enemy is the devil, the harvest is the completion of the age. To disciples who might want to judge now, he says that the angels will sort things out at the end, and that the righteous will shine.
settings.readers: For Matthew's community, the explanation described their own time: between sowing and harvest, wheat and weeds together.

settings.what: The parable of the hidden treasure
settings.to: his disciples, privately
settings.when: the same day, in the house
settings.why: In a land often at war, people hid valuables in the ground, and finding them was a known dream. The finder gladly sells everything to buy the field. The point for disciples who had left everything was joy: the kingdom is worth it.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, who had given up a lot to follow Jesus, heard that it was a joyful trade.

settings.to: his disciples, privately
settings.when: the same day, in the house
settings.why: Pearls were among the most prized luxuries in the Roman world. A merchant who knows pearls finds one of supreme value and sells all he has. Paired with the treasure, it says that the kingdom is worth everything, whether found by chance or after a long search.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers heard the same call: the kingdom is the one thing worth everything.

settings.to: his disciples, privately
settings.when: the same day, in the house
settings.why: Fishermen on the Sea of Galilee used dragnets that caught every kind of fish, clean and unclean, which then had to be sorted (Leviticus 11:9–12). Some disciples were fishermen. The parable, like the weeds, says that sorting belongs to the angels at the end of the age.
settings.readers: For Matthew's readers, the church was like the net: gathering all kinds, with the final sorting left to God.

settings.to: his disciples, privately
settings.when: the same day, in the house
settings.why: Jesus asks whether they have understood, and they say yes. He then describes the disciple as a scribe trained for the kingdom, like a homeowner who brings out new and old things from his storeroom. To men who were not trained scribes, it gave them a teaching role.
settings.readers: Many think Matthew saw himself and his community's teachers in this saying: they held onto the old (the law and prophets) and the new (Jesus' teaching).

settings.what: Jesus' saying about a prophet's hometown
settings.to: the people in the synagogue of his hometown, Nazareth
settings.when: after the parables discourse, on a visit home
settings.why: The townspeople know his family and his trade and cannot accept that he is anything more. Jesus answers with a proverb: a prophet is honored except at home. It places him with the prophets whom Israel rejected.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, rejected by many of their own people, heard that Jesus had been rejected by his.
views: Luke places a fuller version at the start of Jesus' ministry (Luke 4:16–30), with the same proverb.

traditions.q: Should the church try to remove wicked people from its membership, or leave the weeds until the harvest (13:24–30, 36–43)?
views: Augustine taught that the church on earth is a mixed body of good and bad, and that the final separation belongs to God. The Catechism describes the church as holy yet containing sinners, always in need of purification.
The visible church contains both true believers and hypocrites, as the parable shows, but church discipline is still needed for open sin. Westminster teaches that even the purest churches are mixed.
The church is the assembly of believers, but in this life many hypocrites and evil people are mixed with them; the sacraments are still valid when given by unworthy ministers.

The field is the world, not the church (13:38), as Menno Simons argued against Reformers who cited the parable. Hubmaier used it against burning heretics. The church should be a gathered body of believers who keep each other faithful through discipline, including the ban, as the Schleitheim and Dordrecht confessions teach.

Churches should be made up of believers who have been baptized on their own confession. Roger Williams, briefly a Baptist and later a Seeker, also used the parable to argue that governments must not punish people for their religion, since the weeds are to be left until the harvest.
